title: Latency: trace the complete request
objective: Find the stage limiting response time before choosing an optimization.
scenario: Illustrative sequential request: 30 ms network, 70 ms application, 100 ms database.
tradeoff: An index can shorten reads but adds storage and write maintenance; more concurrency can increase waiting.

steps.title: The checkout is slow
steps.caption: A checkout takes 200 ms. Which stage would you change, and what evidence would justify it?
steps.insight: Reason about this scenario before comparing the mechanism and its consequences.

steps.title: Reach the application
steps.caption: The gateway routes the request; connection and network costs belong in the full path.
steps.insight: A fast server-only timer can hide client-observed delay.
detail: Gateway and app have different roles.
Return travel also belongs in timing.

steps.title: Do application work
steps.caption: The application performs 70 ms of its own work, then needs database data.
steps.insight: Optimize the critical path, not a conveniently visible component.

steps.title: Complete the first query
steps.caption: The 100 ms query finishes; the application can build its response.
steps.insight: For this sequential example: 30 + 70 + 100 = 200 ms.

steps.title: Locate the dominant stage
steps.caption: A trace links stages; investigate the database rather than guessing that bandwidth is slow.
steps.insight: Parent spans can include child time; avoid counting it twice.

steps.title: Apply a useful index
steps.caption: A suitable index reduces the illustrative query from 100 ms to 25 ms.
steps.insight: Change the measured bottleneck, then check its costs.
detail: This is not a benchmark promise.

steps.title: Measure the new result
steps.caption: The same path now totals 125 ms, a 37.5% reduction in this example.
steps.insight: Lower request latency and higher throughput are separate measurements.

steps.title: Watch overload separately
steps.caption: More arrivals than capacity build a queue, even after the query improves.
steps.insight: Adding concurrency does not guarantee more completed requests.
detail: Use stable averages for Little's Law.
Bound work or add useful capacity.

title: DNS: lookup, cache, and a server move
objective: Resolve a service name while understanding cached answers during a destination change.
scenario: Illustrative shop.example moves from 203.0.113.8 to 203.0.113.9.
tradeoff: Shorter TTLs can reduce stale routing but increase lookups; existing connections do not instantly migrate.

steps.title: A name but no address
steps.caption: The browser has shop.example but no cached address. Who should it ask, and who owns the answer?
steps.insight: Reason about this scenario before comparing the mechanism and its consequences.

steps.title: Start with a referral
steps.caption: The resolver asks a root server and receives a referral toward the relevant TLD.
steps.insight: The root does not fetch the shop page or run the whole lookup.
detail: Root answers which direction to ask.

steps.title: Find the zone authority
steps.caption: The TLD response directs the resolver to the zone's authoritative nameservers.
steps.insight: Delegation tells the resolver who holds the relevant record.
detail: TLD is not the shop's web server.

steps.title: Read the published record
steps.caption: Authoritative DNS returns 203.0.113.8 and an illustrative 60-second TTL.
steps.insight: The TTL limits normal cache reuse; it is not a page-download timer.
detail: Address and TTL are separate fields.
This TTL is an illustrative value.

steps.title: Return the answer
steps.caption: The resolver supplies the address; the browser can now connect to that endpoint.
steps.insight: Resolving a name and reaching its server are separate steps.

steps.title: Retrieve the page
steps.caption: The browser uses HTTPS with the old web server, which returns the page.
steps.insight: DNS servers do not relay the website's response body.
detail: HTTP response comes from the server.
An open connection can be reused.

steps.title: Publish a server move
steps.caption: The operator changes the authoritative answer to .9, but an existing cache still holds .8.
steps.insight: Changing the source record does not purge every cached answer.

steps.title: A cached lookup stays old
steps.caption: Before expiry, a later lookup can still return .8 and connect to the old endpoint.
steps.insight: Short TTLs reduce cache duration; they do not create instant failover.
detail: No new authority lookup is needed.

steps.title: Refresh after TTL expiry
steps.caption: After the story's TTL expires, the resolver asks again and learns the new .9 address.
steps.insight: Plan changes ahead of time rather than assuming immediate cache replacement.
detail: Story time jumps past TTL expiry.
Cached delegation can still be reused.

steps.title: Use the new endpoint
steps.caption: The browser connects to the new server and receives a page from .9.
steps.insight: Measure DNS answers and server reachability independently during a move.

title: TCP and UDP: what a loss changes
objective: Match delivery and ordering behavior to an application's timing requirements.
scenario: Illustrative file bytes 1-3 and voice frames A-C each suffer one lost item.
tradeoff: Ordered recovery can delay later bytes; avoiding transport waits leaves more delivery policy to the application.

steps.title: Two different deadlines
steps.caption: A file and voice call each lose data. Should both wait for recovery?
steps.insight: Reason about this scenario before comparing the mechanism and its consequences.
detail: Which data still has value if late?

steps.title: TCP delivers initial bytes
steps.caption: The first TCP bytes arrive and become available to the file reader.
steps.insight: TCP presents a byte stream, not application message boundaries.

steps.title: A TCP gap holds later data
steps.caption: Range 2 is lost; range 3 arrives but waits behind the missing bytes.
steps.insight: Ordered delivery can make a later arrival wait for earlier lost data.
detail: The sender detects or times out loss.

steps.title: TCP retransmits the gap
steps.caption: Recovery supplies range 2, allowing the reader to consume ranges 2 and 3 in order.
steps.insight: Recovery costs time and network work; the connection can still eventually fail.
detail: Delivery does not prove business commit.
TCP can report errors or time out.

steps.title: UDP exposes an early frame
steps.caption: Frame A reaches the UDP receiver and is available to the voice application.
steps.insight: UDP supplies datagrams without built-in ordering or retransmission.

steps.title: One UDP frame disappears
steps.caption: Frame B is lost, but C can arrive without UDP waiting for B.
steps.insight: A missing datagram does not impose TCP's ordered-stream wait.
detail: UDP does not repair the loss itself.
C may still be late for playback.

steps.title: The application chooses
steps.caption: The voice player can conceal a gap or drop late sound according to its timing policy.
steps.insight: Less transport waiting shifts responsibility toward application design.
detail: Recovery can be added above UDP.
Live deadlines differ from file goals.

steps.title: Design the whole protocol
steps.caption: Check congestion handling, message size, loss behavior, and the application's own success response.
steps.insight: Neither UDP nor TCP alone establishes that a payment or other business operation succeeded.
detail: Do not equate UDP with always faster.
Measure under realistic loss and load.

title: Load balancing: healthy routing and shared state
objective: Spread requests while preserving sessions and handling instance failure.
scenario: Two application instances share user 7's session and one database.
tradeoff: Shared state permits flexible routing but remains a dependency; extra app instances do not scale the database.

steps.title: A request changes servers
steps.caption: A customer's next request reaches another server. Where must session state live?
steps.insight: Reason about this scenario before comparing the mechanism and its consequences.
detail: What if the selected app crashes?
Which shared store can still fail?

steps.title: Route the first request
steps.caption: The client reaches the balancer, which selects ready instance A.
steps.insight: A routing rule should match the workload and health information.
detail: Round robin is one possible policy.

steps.title: Read the session
steps.caption: App A obtains user 7's shared session and checks permissions before doing business work.
steps.insight: Shared lookup lets another instance continue later without relying on A's memory.
detail: Session ID is not blanket permission.

steps.title: Finish business work
steps.caption: A queries the database and sends its response back through the balancer.
steps.insight: A complete topology includes data access and the response path.
detail: Adding apps does not double DB capacity.

steps.title: An instance fails
steps.caption: A stops responding; readiness checks remove it from new routing.
steps.insight: Detection and rerouting take time; in-flight work can have uncertain outcomes.
detail: A failed request may need safe retry.

steps.title: Route the next request
steps.caption: A later request reaches B rather than the failed instance.
steps.insight: Multiple instances help only when routing actually avoids unusable ones.

steps.title: Recover the same session
steps.caption: B loads user 7's existing shared state instead of inventing a new session.
steps.insight: External session state supports movement between application instances.
detail: Sticky routing is a different choice.
Memory on failed A is not durable.

steps.title: Return through B
steps.caption: B performs the query and returns a response through the same service entry point.
steps.insight: Measure successful end-to-end work, not merely balanced request counts.
detail: Shared DB can become the bottleneck.
Healthy B still needs its dependencies.

steps.title: A shared dependency fails
steps.caption: The session store becomes unavailable, so adding app instances cannot repair session access.
steps.insight: Shared state can remove instance affinity while introducing a shared failure point.
detail: Do not bypass authorization on failure.

steps.title: Recover safely
steps.caption: Once session access recovers, B can resume authorized requests; monitor the whole dependency path.
steps.insight: Capacity, state placement, and failure handling must be designed together.

title: Cache-aside: speed, stale copies, and recovery
objective: Reduce repeated database work without treating cached data as automatically current.
scenario: Illustrative product 42 changes from price 500 to 550 while invalidation fails.
tradeoff: Cache hits reduce repeated work, but failures and races require freshness rules, memory, and additional coordination.

steps.title: A fast page changes price
steps.caption: A popular product changes price. How can repeated reads stay fast without silently using an unacceptable old value?
steps.insight: Reason about this scenario before comparing the mechanism and its consequences.

steps.title: Observe a cache miss
steps.caption: The reader asks the cache and learns that no value is available.
steps.insight: A miss is normal behavior, not automatically a service failure.
detail: Do not confuse miss with cache outage.
A miss still needs database work.

steps.title: Read the authoritative value
steps.caption: The application reads price 500 from the database, rather than asking the cache to load it.
steps.insight: Cache-aside places the loading decision in application code.
detail: The database is still the authority.

steps.title: Fill and return
steps.caption: The application caches the value and returns price 500 to the client.
steps.insight: The cache now helps later requests reuse work.
detail: Choose an appropriate key and TTL.
Include inputs that change the result.

steps.title: Serve a later hit
steps.caption: Another read uses the cached 500 without repeating the database query.
steps.insight: Measure avoided origin work and latency, not hit rate alone.
detail: A hit does not prove freshness.

steps.title: Commit a new price
steps.caption: The writer commits 550; until invalidation succeeds, the cached 500 is old.
steps.insight: A database commit and cache invalidation are separate failure boundaries.
detail: Old entries can outlive a write.

steps.title: Invalidation fails
steps.caption: The writer cannot remove the old entry, although the database update already succeeded.
steps.insight: An invalidation recipe needs recovery behavior as well as a happy path.

steps.title: A hit can now be wrong
steps.caption: The next product-page read returns cached 500 unless its freshness policy prevents it.
steps.insight: A checkout must enforce its actual payable price through an authoritative rule.
detail: TTL does not imply immediate freshness.

steps.title: Repair the copy
steps.caption: A successful purge lets the next miss reload 550 and replace the old cached value.
steps.insight: Recovery must eventually make stale copies converge under the chosen policy.
detail: Concurrent stale fills still need rules.
Version checks can support stronger rules.

steps.title: Protect the miss path
steps.caption: If many callers miss together, bound reload work and protect database capacity.
steps.insight: A cache adds capacity only when failure and miss behavior remain controlled.
detail: Test total cache loss and hot keys.

title: Replication: write, lag, read, and restore
objective: Use data copies for reads and recovery while recognizing lag and propagated mistakes.
scenario: An address changes from V1 to V2; a later accidental deletion reaches both live copies.
tradeoff: Asynchronous copies can lag; waiting for acknowledgements costs latency, and historical backups still need restore testing.

steps.title: One update, two views
steps.caption: An address changes, but a reader sees its old value. Which copies and timing could explain that?
steps.insight: Reason about this scenario before comparing the mechanism and its consequences.
detail: When may the writer see success?
Can a copy preserve an old mistake?

steps.title: Commit without waiting
steps.caption: The primary commits V2 and acknowledges under this example's asynchronous replication policy.
steps.insight: An acknowledged primary write need not already be applied on every replica.

steps.title: Read during lag
steps.caption: A reader queries the replica before the change arrives and receives V1.
steps.insight: Route reads according to their required freshness, not merely lower load.
detail: Old read is possible during lag.
A healthy replica can still be stale.

steps.title: Apply the change
steps.caption: The replication stream carries V2 to the replica, which applies it.
steps.insight: Asynchronous replication has a propagation stage that may take variable time.

steps.title: Read after catch-up
steps.caption: A later replica read sees V2 after the change has been applied.
steps.insight: Eventual visibility depends on successful propagation and application.
detail: A particular read can still race updates.
No promise of instant equal state.

steps.title: Choose a fresher path
steps.caption: A freshness-sensitive read uses the appropriate authoritative path instead of an arbitrary lagging copy.
steps.insight: Read guarantees require a complete routing and consistency protocol.
detail: Waiting for replicas can cost latency.

steps.title: Delete the wrong data
steps.caption: An accidental deletion commits on the primary; live replication does not know it was a mistake.
steps.insight: More live copies do not automatically preserve older correct data.
detail: Bad writes can be valid database work.

steps.title: Copy the mistake too
steps.caption: The deletion propagates, so both primary and replica now lack the address.
steps.insight: Replication is not a substitute for historical recovery.
detail: Restore points may lose newer changes.

steps.title: Test an isolated restore
steps.caption: The backup restores V1 in a sandbox, proving which historical data that restore point can recover.
steps.insight: A usable backup requires a tested restore procedure and explicit recovery objectives.
detail: Restore is isolated from live writes.
V2 is newer than this snapshot.
Record restore time and lost changes.

title: Transactions: two buyers and the final ticket
objective: Prevent concurrent reservation requests from both claiming the last available unit.
scenario: Illustrative product 42 starts with one ticket; two buyers submit together.
tradeoff: Correct conditional writes need suitable database concurrency behavior; external payment remains a separate coordination boundary.

steps.title: The last ticket
steps.caption: Two customers click Buy for the last ticket. Which database action should decide the winner?
steps.insight: Reason about this scenario before comparing the mechanism and its consequences.
detail: Is reading stock already a reservation?
Which condition must be checked together?

steps.title: Two requests overlap
steps.caption: A and B reach the reservation service before either has a confirmed result.
steps.insight: Concurrency is about overlapping work, even with one visible service endpoint.
detail: One API can handle concurrent calls.
A read is not yet a reservation.

steps.title: See the unsafe choice
steps.caption: Separate read-then-write checks can let both callers observe stock 1.
steps.insight: A transaction wrapper alone does not settle the isolation behavior.
detail: Do not confirm from a stale read.

steps.title: Use an atomic condition
steps.caption: Instead, update this product only while quantity is positive.
steps.insight: Scope the update to the product and check the actual write result.

steps.title: Commit A's reservation
steps.caption: The database changes one row and commits stock plus its related reservation consistently.
steps.insight: Only the successful committed result may justify A's confirmation.
detail: Reverse arrival can let B win.
Keep related changes in one transaction.

steps.title: Reject B's stock change
steps.caption: B's condition now finds no positive quantity, so it changes zero rows.
steps.insight: The loser must not receive a success response for a reservation it did not obtain.

steps.title: Separate the payment
steps.caption: A's payment call crosses another service boundary; a local transaction cannot atomically cover it.
steps.insight: Do not hold a local row lock while assuming an external charge shares the same commit.

steps.title: Resolve external outcomes
steps.caption: A payment failure or unknown result needs a defined recovery or reservation-expiry policy.
steps.insight: Correct stock allocation and correct charging are related but distinct invariants.
detail: A timeout does not prove no charge.

steps.title: Verify the whole result
steps.caption: Test simultaneous requests and interruptions; confirm no extra ticket or duplicate side effect appears.
steps.insight: Measure correctness under races, not only successful sequential requests.

title: Normalize current facts; preserve historical snapshots
objective: Choose data ownership and duplication according to the meaning of each fact.
scenario: Customer 7 moves from address A to B after an order shipped to A.
tradeoff: Joins can add read work; duplicated current values need coordinated updates, while historical snapshots intentionally preserve past meaning.

steps.title: A move after delivery
steps.caption: A customer moves after an order ships. Which address should current-profile and past-order screens display?
steps.insight: Reason about this scenario before comparing the mechanism and its consequences.
detail: Are these fields the same fact?
When should a snapshot be captured?

steps.title: Read the current profile
steps.caption: When the order is created, the service reads customer 7's chosen delivery address A.
steps.insight: Capture a purchase fact at a deliberate business boundary.

steps.title: Record a reference and fact
steps.caption: The order stores customer ID 7 and delivery snapshot A as part of its creation.
steps.insight: A reference identifies the customer; a snapshot records the order's own historical value.
detail: These are tables, not separate commits.
Define when the order becomes visible.

steps.title: Change today's profile
steps.caption: The customer later updates the profile address from A to B.
steps.insight: Updating the current owner need not rewrite historical order data.
detail: One profile update changes current truth.
Order snapshot still means purchase A.

steps.title: Display the current value
steps.caption: The current profile view reads B from its owner rather than maintaining an accidental extra copy.
steps.insight: Normalized ownership avoids updating many copies of the same current fact.
detail: A join or lookup can add read work.

steps.title: Display the old delivery
steps.caption: The past-order view reads snapshot A, correctly preserving where that order was sent.
steps.insight: Historical A and current B can both be correct at the same time.
detail: Do not infer inconsistency from values.

steps.title: Avoid a blind propagation
steps.caption: Changing every address copy to B would corrupt the order's purchase-time meaning.
steps.insight: An update policy must follow semantics, not a rule to replace every matching value.
detail: A snapshot is not a stale profile.

steps.title: Decide on denormalization
steps.caption: If a live read becomes expensive, consider a derived copy only with an owner and update policy.
steps.insight: Denormalization trades read cost for write and propagation complexity.

title: Sharding: route by ownership, then handle growth
objective: Divide a dataset while accounting for routing, replication, hot shards, and cross-shard queries.
scenario: Illustrative customer ranges 1-1000 and 1001-2000 live on different shards.
tradeoff: Targeted reads can scale, but skew, rebalancing, and cross-shard coordination add complexity; sharding alone is not redundancy.

nodes.label: Shard router
nodes.role: Map key to an owning shard

steps.title: Outgrow one database
steps.caption: Customer traffic outgrows one database. How should a request find its owner without querying every machine?
steps.insight: Reason about this scenario before comparing the mechanism and its consequences.
detail: Does a copy own a different range?

steps.title: Use the customer's key
steps.caption: Customer 42 reaches the router, which selects A from the range map.
steps.insight: A suitable shard key can keep one customer's related work local.
detail: Route by an explicit ownership rule.
A key is not merely a random label.

steps.title: Return the local result
steps.caption: A returns the customer's data without asking B to scan its unrelated range.
steps.insight: Sharding helps targeted work when queries know the partition key.

steps.title: Route another owner
steps.caption: Customer 1500 instead goes to B and receives B's result.
steps.insight: B is another owner, not an interchangeable replica of A.
detail: Data model and routing must agree.

steps.title: Copy A independently
steps.caption: A's changes propagate to its replica while B continues owning a different dataset.
steps.insight: Availability requires deliberate replicas and failover, not just more distinct shards.
detail: Replica lag still needs a policy.

steps.title: Run a cross-range query
steps.caption: The reporting service needs both ranges, so the router fans out and merges the results.
steps.insight: A fast single-key read does not make global joins or totals free.

steps.title: Notice a hot customer
steps.caption: A celebrity customer overloads A even though both shards contain similar customer counts.
steps.insight: Balance actual traffic and data, not just the number of keys.
detail: One hot key can dominate requests.
More B capacity does not help A.

steps.title: Plan growth and movement
steps.caption: Changing ownership needs a migration plan that keeps routing and data location compatible.
steps.insight: Rebalancing is an operational process, not a label on a diagram.

steps.title: Compare the alternatives
steps.caption: Improve queries first; split by domain only when billing and catalog need functional separation.
steps.insight: Customer-key sharding differs from a domain split or a federated query layer.

title: Consistent hashing: placement and membership changes
objective: Limit key remapping when storage or cache membership changes.
scenario: Illustrative K at 170 moves from C to new node D at 200.
tradeoff: Limited movement reduces disruption, but membership agreement, data transfer, skew, replication, and recovery remain separate responsibilities.

steps.title: A member joins
steps.caption: A cache node joins. Which keys must move, and how will clients find the new owners?
steps.insight: Reason about this scenario before comparing the mechanism and its consequences.
detail: Does a new map move actual data?
What if clients hold an old map?

steps.title: Find the old owner
steps.caption: Key K at 170 reaches C at 260 first; the router sends K's request there.
steps.insight: Ownership follows the ring rule even when another server looks physically nearer.
detail: K is after B and before C.

steps.title: See a key that differs
steps.caption: Key Q at 80 reaches B at 140 and is served independently.
steps.insight: Different key positions can have different owners on the same ring.
detail: The router does not contact all nodes.

steps.title: Add a new member
steps.caption: D joins at 200, splitting part of C's previous ownership range.
steps.insight: A new member changes only its affected successor range under this scheme.
detail: Up to and including 200 maps to D.

steps.title: Move the affected data
steps.caption: K at 170 moves from C to D; migration must make its data available at the new owner.
steps.insight: A new mapping alone does not transfer the stored value.
detail: Copy data before relying on new owner.

steps.title: Route using the new view
steps.caption: The updated router now selects D for K, while Q still belongs to B.
steps.insight: The benefit is limited key movement, not a guarantee of perfectly even load.
detail: Q at 80 still maps to B.
K at 170 now meets D first.

steps.title: Handle a stale map
steps.caption: A client using old membership may still contact C, so migration needs a compatibility policy.
steps.insight: Membership convergence and data migration are separate operational concerns.
detail: Do not assume instant map agreement.

steps.title: Account for hot keys
steps.caption: Virtual nodes can balance ranges, but one extremely popular key can still overload its owner.
steps.insight: Consistent hashing reduces remapping; it does not remove skew or provide recovery automatically.
detail: Replicas and hot-key handling are extra.

title: Bloom filters: a cheap gate, not the authority
objective: Avoid expensive absent-key reads without mistaking possible membership for actual membership.
scenario: Illustrative 12-bit filter: A and missing X share positions 1, 4, and 8.
tradeoff: Space-efficient negatives save reads, but positives need verification and filter maintenance must cover the actual queried data.

nodes.label: Hash functions
nodes.role: Map a key to bit positions

steps.title: Skip unnecessary reads?
steps.caption: Most requested keys do not exist. Can a small precheck avoid disk reads without inventing membership?
steps.insight: Reason about this scenario before comparing the mechanism and its consequences.
detail: Which result can safely skip storage?
What if two keys share positions?
What if an insertion is missing?

steps.title: Insert a real item
steps.caption: The writer stores A, then its hash positions 1, 4, and 8 are represented in the filter.
steps.insight: Insertion sets shared bits; it does not store a unique full record in each bit.
detail: Use the same hashes when querying.
Keep insertions and filter state aligned.

steps.title: Probe a missing position
steps.caption: Query Y needs positions 2, 6, and 10; a required zero proves absence from the represented set.
steps.insight: A negative can avoid disk work only when the filter covers the relevant current data.
detail: This conclusion is about represented data.

steps.title: Skip the costly lookup
steps.caption: With a current filter, Y is definitely absent, so this query does not reach the store.
steps.insight: Cheap negative results are where the saved authoritative reads come from.
detail: Every request still pays filter cost.

steps.title: Probe a colliding key
steps.caption: Different key X also maps to 1, 4, and 8, all already set by A.
steps.insight: Shared positions allow false positives; all set bits do not prove the key exists.
detail: X was never inserted in this example.
Bit positions do not identify the key.

steps.title: Verify maybe in storage
steps.caption: The client queries the authoritative store, which confirms that X does not exist.
steps.insight: A Bloom positive is permission to check, not a reason to reject a username as taken.
detail: This one false positive costs a lookup.

steps.title: Tune memory and work
steps.caption: Choose capacity and acceptable false positives; overfilling a fixed filter increases wasted lookups.
steps.insight: More bits reduce collision pressure, but hashing and memory both have costs.
detail: No arbitrary bit clearing for deletes.
Shared bits may belong to other items.
Rebuild or use a suitable variant.

steps.title: Expose a maintenance gap
steps.caption: A new item reaches storage but its filter update is delayed; trusting a negative can miss real data.
steps.insight: The no-false-negative property assumes the queried set has actually been inserted.
detail: Stale filter differs from false positive.
Update lag can become a correctness bug.

steps.title: Bypass until repaired
steps.caption: When coverage is uncertain, consult the store and restore the filter's maintenance guarantees.
steps.insight: Use the optimization only when it preserves the operation's correctness.
detail: Track memory, false positives, and reads.

title: CAP: compare two partition policies
objective: Reason about strong consistency and availability when replicas cannot communicate.
scenario: Two ticket replicas lose communication while clients still reach their own regional copy.
tradeoff: During a partition, answering at every non-failing node conflicts with one latest global state; refusal protects coordination at availability cost.

steps.title: Two sides cannot talk
steps.caption: Two reachable ticket replicas cannot communicate. Can both answer every request and still promise one latest shared state?
steps.insight: Reason about this scenario before comparing the mechanism and its consequences.
detail: Can B know A's newest write?
What must a confirmed sale mean?
When is refusal safer than guessing?

steps.title: Break communication
steps.caption: A and B can no longer coordinate even though both processes continue running.
steps.insight: A network partition is not the same as a crashed database process.
detail: Local nodes cannot know remote updates.

steps.title: Availability-first branch
steps.caption: In this branch, A accepts and acknowledges a sale without waiting for B.
steps.insight: Acknowledging a write in isolation requires confronting what another reachable copy can safely answer.
detail: B has not learned the new value.

steps.title: B must answer somehow
steps.caption: Client B asks after A's acknowledged sale; B cannot confirm A's current state.
steps.insight: The request reaches a non-failing node; missing coordination is the problem.
detail: Local health does not supply new facts.

steps.title: Answer with old information
steps.caption: Returning B's available value serves the request but can violate the chosen strong-consistency guarantee.
steps.insight: Availability-first behavior needs an explicit tolerance for stale or conflicting outcomes.
detail: Do not treat this as safe ticket sale.

steps.title: Rewind: require agreement
steps.caption: Compare an alternative protocol: require both toy replicas to agree before confirming the same sale.
steps.insight: These are alternative policies, not a safe mid-operation switch of guarantees.
detail: Toy commit rule needs both replicas.

steps.title: Coordination-first waits
steps.caption: A cannot confirm the sale; B refuses a fresh result while the agreement path is broken.
steps.insight: Refusing or waiting protects the coordination rule but sacrifices CAP availability for these requests.
detail: CAP availability is not monthly uptime.

steps.title: Heal and finish safely
steps.caption: After communication returns, the coordinated sale can be agreed and acknowledged.
steps.insight: Recovery enables coordination; the operation's protocol defines when completion is safe.
detail: Do not invent an unsafe local commit.

steps.title: Choose per requirement
steps.caption: Define which operations tolerate stale answers and which must refuse when required coordination is unavailable.
steps.insight: A category label is less useful than a precise operation and failure response.
detail: The two branches have different costs.

title: PACELC: healthy-path latency and partition policy
objective: Choose normal-operation freshness and coordination costs as well as behavior during a partition.
scenario: Compare illustrative 40 ms coordinated and 5 ms local acknowledgements.
tradeoff: Remote coordination can cost latency; earlier local acknowledgements require explicit remote-read and partition behavior.

steps.title: Ask about the healthy path
steps.caption: Even without a partition, must a remote reader immediately see this newly acknowledged update?
steps.insight: Requirements determine which communication the whole read/write protocol must perform.
detail: When may the writer see success?

steps.title: Coordinate before success
steps.caption: In one illustrative protocol, the local write waits for the remote coordination rule.
steps.insight: Waiting buys only the guarantees of the complete protocol, not a universal consistency label.

steps.title: Acknowledge the chosen rule
steps.caption: Remote coordination completes and the writer receives the illustrative 40 ms acknowledgement.
steps.insight: A distant stage can increase healthy-operation write latency.
detail: One remote ACK alone is not a proof.

steps.title: Compare a local-first path
steps.caption: Rewind the example: another policy acknowledges local V2 before the remote copy catches up.
steps.insight: These toy 5 ms and 40 ms values compare policies, not benchmark products.
detail: The remote copy can now lag.

steps.title: Read from the lagging copy
steps.caption: A remote read may still return V1 after the earlier local acknowledgement.
steps.insight: Earlier acknowledgement needs an explicit rule for subsequent reads.
detail: A healthy network can still have lag.

steps.title: Route a stronger read
steps.caption: A selected authoritative read path can obtain V2, with its own communication and availability costs.
steps.insight: Strong reads depend on protocol and routing, not the mere existence of synchronous or asynchronous copies.
detail: Account for distance on this path.
Do not let arbitrary replicas bypass it.

steps.title: Catch up the remote copy
steps.caption: The asynchronous stream eventually applies V2 on the distant database.

updates.r: Remote view can now catch up

steps.insight: Propagation and read rules together determine observable freshness.

steps.title: Now partition the replicas
steps.caption: When communication stops, decide whether the next operation can complete without required coordination.
steps.insight: Partition availability versus consistency is a different question from healthy-path latency.
detail: Some operations may refuse or wait.

steps.title: Specify both decisions
steps.caption: Document partition behavior and normal-operation latency/freshness for the actual operations and protocol.
steps.insight: PACELC prompts both failure-path and healthy-path reasoning.

title: Saga: local commits and compensating recovery
objective: Recover a multi-service operation when an earlier committed step must be compensated.
scenario: An order charges once, stock is unavailable, and a refund response is lost.
tradeoff: Local commits avoid one global transaction but expose intermediate states and require durable retries, reconciliation, and compensation.

steps.title: Begin with a business risk
steps.caption: What should happen if charging succeeds but the later stock reservation cannot complete?
steps.insight: Each service has its own commit boundary; partial success must be represented honestly.
detail: What must survive a coordinator crash?
What status should the customer see?

steps.title: Persist a pending order
steps.caption: The coordinator records the order and recoverable step identifiers before advancing.
steps.insight: A durable workflow can distinguish accepted work from a fully finished purchase.

steps.title: Charge once and record it
steps.caption: The payment operation succeeds; the coordinator durably records that completed local step.
steps.insight: An earlier local commit does not disappear when a different service later fails.
detail: Provider must support safe retry behavior.

steps.title: Stock reservation fails
steps.caption: The stock service reports no inventory, so the charged order cannot proceed normally.
steps.insight: A saga must define compensation for already completed effects.
detail: This is not one database rollback.

steps.title: Record the refund intent
steps.caption: The coordinator persists a refund-needed state with a stable compensation identifier.
steps.insight: Intent must remain recoverable if the process stops before the next call.
detail: Compensation can fail or take time.

steps.title: Lose the refund response
steps.caption: The provider refunds under key RK, but its result does not reach the coordinator.
steps.insight: A timeout is not proof that the refund did not happen.
detail: This provider dedupes refund key RK.

steps.title: Resume from durable state
steps.caption: The recovery worker finds the unfinished saga and resumes the same compensation, not a new logical refund.
steps.insight: Safe recovery follows durable progress rather than in-memory assumptions.

steps.title: Confirm the same refund
steps.caption: A retry or status lookup confirms RK's existing result, which the coordinator records.
steps.insight: The provider contract and local recovery state must agree on the operation's identity.
detail: No second logical refund is requested.

steps.title: Report the truthful result
steps.caption: The customer sees the order failed and its payment was refunded; some external effects may still remain.
steps.insight: Compensation restores a business outcome; it is not time travel or erasure of every side effect.
detail: A receipt email may still exist.
Test every crash and retry boundary.

title: Cache eviction: replay LRU and FIFO
objective: Free limited cache memory using a deliberate reuse policy without confusing eviction with freshness.
scenario: Compare two alternative caches holding three equally sized entries under the same access trace.
tradeoff: LRU tracks recency; FIFO is simpler. Reuse, object size, metadata cost, and freshness require separate evaluation.

nodes.label: Access driver
nodes.initial: Insert A, B, C; then read A

steps.title: Start with limited memory
steps.caption: Two alternative three-entry caches receive the same workload; which old item should make room for D?
steps.insight: The useful choice depends on how past accesses predict future reuse.
detail: Entries are equally sized in this toy.

steps.title: Fill both alternatives
steps.caption: Insert A, B, and C in that order; both caches initially contain the same entries.
steps.insight: Equal contents can conceal different internal policy state.

steps.title: Read A again
steps.caption: Both caches hit A; LRU updates recency while FIFO retains its insertion order.
steps.insight: A read changes the eviction decision only for policies that use that information.

steps.title: Miss on the new D
steps.caption: D is absent and must be loaded from the origin before insertion.
steps.insight: A new value requires an admission and space decision.
detail: Cache miss still costs origin work.
D is not yet in either cache.

steps.title: LRU removes B
steps.caption: LRU evicts B, now the least recently used entry, and admits D.
steps.insight: Recently reread A survives in LRU under this exact trace.
detail: B was last used before C and A.
This is not a universal best policy.

steps.title: FIFO removes A
steps.caption: FIFO evicts A, the earliest inserted entry, despite the recent successful read.
steps.insight: FIFO's simplicity means recency does not influence its victim.

steps.title: Read A next
steps.caption: LRU hits A; FIFO misses and needs an origin read for this next operation.

updates.l: A hit; order C, D, A

steps.insight: Compare real traces, origin requests, and tracking overhead instead of policy names.
detail: Other traces can favor other policies.
Huge values also affect memory use.

steps.title: Separate memory from truth
steps.caption: If A changes at the origin, its surviving cached copy can still hold an old value.
steps.insight: Eviction frees memory; TTLs and update/invalidation rules address freshness.

steps.title: Tune for the real workload
steps.caption: Measure hit rate, byte capacity, miss latency, origin work, and policy bookkeeping under representative accesses.
steps.insight: Choose policy and admission separately from the application's acceptable staleness.
detail: Consider object size and frequency aging.
Test cost, not only hit percentage.

title: Idempotency: retries, durable state, and recovery
objective: Prevent repeated requests from creating repeated effects while recovering uncertain outcomes.
scenario: An illustrative 500-unit payment succeeds, its response disappears, and the caller retries.
tradeoff: Durable deduplication adds state and coordination; safe recovery must cover the external side effect, not merely store a key.

steps.title: Start with the uncertainty
steps.caption: A payment response can disappear after the money moves. What should a retry mean?
steps.insight: The operation's identity must survive a lost response and simultaneous retries.
detail: Which state must survive a crash?
Who can confirm the provider outcome?

steps.title: Validate and claim K
steps.caption: The API scopes K to its caller and operation, validates the body, then atomically claims a durable record.
steps.insight: A check followed by an unprotected insert can race; use a suitable atomic uniqueness rule.

steps.title: A duplicate arrives early
steps.caption: A simultaneous same-body request finds K already pending rather than becoming a second owner.
steps.insight: Define in-progress behavior; not every duplicate already has a completed result.
detail: Do not report an unperformed charge.

steps.title: Perform the external step
steps.caption: The winning operation uses a stable provider identifier; its charge result is durably associated with K.
steps.insight: Local records and external effects require one coherent retry and reconciliation design.
detail: Store enough state for crash recovery.

steps.title: Lose the final response
steps.caption: The API sends success, but the client never receives it.
steps.insight: A transport timeout does not prove that the business operation failed.
detail: The caller still needs a safe answer.

steps.title: Return the existing result
steps.caption: Retrying K with the same body reads its stored result instead of creating a new charge.
steps.insight: Idempotent handling ties repeated requests to the same logical operation.
detail: No new provider operation is needed.

steps.title: Reject a changed request
steps.caption: Reusing K with a different amount fails the fingerprint rule instead of silently reusing or changing the payment.
steps.insight: A deduplication key needs an explicit meaning, not merely string equality.
detail: Never silently create a second effect.

steps.title: Rewind to a crash boundary
steps.caption: Compare another crash point: K is pending and the provider outcome is not recorded locally.
steps.insight: Skipping every pending key can lose real work; blindly repeating the effect can duplicate it.
detail: Rewind to a different crash boundary.
A pending claim is not proof of success.

steps.title: Reconcile the pending work
steps.caption: Recovery resumes K and resolves the provider's existing outcome using its safe retry or status contract.
steps.insight: A key-only table does not close the crash gap around an external side effect.
detail: Do not invent a new payment identity.

steps.title: Return a truthful outcome
steps.caption: The API returns the resolved result or a documented pending state while recovery continues.
steps.insight: Test duplicate arrivals and every crash boundary, not only a repeated successful response.
detail: Do not expire keys too early.
The invariant is per logical attempt.

title: Token bucket: protect shared search capacity
objective: Protect a service from sustained overload while allowing a controlled burst.
scenario: A customer sends four search requests in one burst.
tradeoff: Burst capacity helps normal clients, but shared accounting adds a dependency and an outage policy.

steps.title: Define the budget
steps.caption: One shared bucket limits this customer across all gateway instances.
steps.insight: A local bucket per instance can multiply a supposedly global allowance.

steps.title: Spend one token
steps.caption: Request one atomically changes the bucket from three tokens to two.
steps.insight: Checking and decrementing must be one coordinated decision.

steps.title: Do useful work
steps.caption: Search reads its index and returns the first result.
steps.insight: The limiter protects downstream capacity rather than speeding up individual queries.

steps.title: Use the burst allowance
steps.caption: Two more immediate requests spend the remaining tokens.
steps.insight: Capacity permits a bounded burst; refill sets the sustained allowance.
detail: No model time passes in this burst

steps.title: Reject excess work
steps.caption: The fourth immediate request finds no token.
steps.insight: Reject before the expensive stage becomes overloaded.
detail: This policy rejects rather than queues

steps.title: Tell the caller clearly
steps.caption: The gateway returns 429; the client backs off instead of hammering.
steps.insight: Fast immediate retries would amplify the original overload.

steps.title: Advance the model clock
steps.caption: One logical second later, one token is available again.
steps.insight: Displayed step timing is illustrative; a real limiter uses actual elapsed time.

steps.title: Admit a later retry
steps.caption: A later request spends the new token and reaches search.
steps.insight: Choose a shared-store failure policy explicitly; fail-open and fail-closed have different costs.

title: Live updates: compare complete connection lifecycles
objective: Deliver timely updates with the required direction and a plan for missed events.
scenario: A browser receives scores or exchanges collaborative editor changes.
tradeoff: Persistent connections reduce repeated setup but need bounded buffers, reconnect handling, and suitable proxy behavior.

nodes.label: Long-poll handler
nodes.role: One held response at a time

steps.title: Choose an interaction
steps.caption: These are alternative transports, not three required services.
steps.insight: Match message direction, frequency, and client constraints before choosing.

steps.title: Hold a long poll
steps.caption: The browser sends a request; the server holds its response.
steps.insight: A server update still needs an outstanding client request in this pattern.
detail: The next request must be opened

steps.title: Reply, then ask again
steps.caption: An update completes the response; the browser starts the next poll.
steps.insight: Repeated waiting requests emulate timely push without one permanently duplex channel.

steps.title: Stream with SSE
steps.caption: In the SSE alternative, one HTTP response carries successive server events.
steps.insight: SSE is a server-to-client event stream, not a bidirectional message channel.

steps.title: Open a WebSocket
steps.caption: In the WebSocket alternative, setup creates a persistent two-way channel.
steps.insight: Connection setup and application message meaning are separate concerns.

steps.title: Send both directions
steps.caption: The browser submits an edit; the service sends its resulting update.
steps.insight: One channel can carry independent messages in both directions.
detail: Do not block all slow clients

steps.title: A connection breaks
steps.caption: The browser disconnects; transport alone cannot preserve unseen events.
steps.insight: A live channel is not itself a durable message history.

steps.title: Recover missing state
steps.caption: After backoff, the browser requests events after 44 or reloads a snapshot.
steps.insight: Define recovery at the application level, regardless of transport.

title: Work queues: absorb bursts and survive worker crashes
objective: Decouple uploads from thumbnail processing without duplicating the durable result.
scenario: A thumbnail worker crashes after saving output but before acknowledgement.
tradeoff: A queue absorbs bursts but adds waiting and cannot solve a sustained processing-capacity deficit.

steps.title: Accept work durably
steps.caption: The upload service enqueues a stable thumbnail job.
steps.insight: Do not claim durable acceptance before the selected handoff actually guarantees it.
detail: The image itself must be durable

steps.title: Return before processing
steps.caption: The uploader receives acceptance while the thumbnail remains pending.
steps.insight: Asynchronous completion shortens the initiating request, not the total work.

steps.title: One worker receives it
steps.caption: Worker A receives J42 under the queue acknowledgement policy.
steps.insight: Competing workers share work; one delivery is not a lifetime exactly-once guarantee.

steps.title: Save the durable result
steps.caption: A creates thumbnail 42 and receives a storage acknowledgement.
steps.insight: A deterministic output key makes a repeat recognizable.

steps.title: Crash before acknowledgement
steps.caption: A crashes before acknowledging; J42 remains unacknowledged.
steps.insight: The queue cannot infer a successful business effect from a missing acknowledgement.

steps.title: Redeliver to another worker
steps.caption: After the applicable timeout, B receives the same J42.
steps.insight: This is the same logical job, not a new thumbnail request.
detail: Do not blindly create another effect

steps.title: Recognize finished work
steps.caption: B verifies the existing complete output instead of conflicting with it.
steps.insight: Deduplication and the durable side effect need a coherent recovery rule.
detail: A marker alone may not prove success

steps.title: Complete and monitor
steps.caption: B safely acknowledges J42; the queue can retire it.
steps.insight: Scale consumers against backlog age and downstream capacity, not queue length alone.

title: Pub/sub: one event, independent business reactions
objective: Let independent consumers react to an order without sharing one competing-work queue.
scenario: Billing and shipping must each process OrderPlaced, even if one is temporarily offline.
tradeoff: Independent subscriptions decouple consumers but require retention, retry, ordering, and schema rules.

steps.title: Publish the business fact
steps.caption: The order service publishes E42 with a stable event identity.
steps.insight: Coordinate the order record and publish handoff; an outbox can bridge that failure boundary.

steps.title: Fan out logically
steps.caption: Billing and shipping each receive independent delivery state.
steps.insight: Fan-out differs from workers competing for one shared job.
detail: Push or pull depends on product

steps.title: Pick one billing worker
steps.caption: A worker receives the billing delivery and begins its action.
steps.insight: Multiple workers may share one subscription without stealing shippingâ€™s event.

steps.title: Commit billing once
steps.caption: The billing worker records its effect and acknowledges.
steps.insight: An acknowledgement follows the durable effect under the chosen processing contract.
detail: Billing has its own retry policy

steps.title: Shipping is still behind
steps.caption: Shipping is offline while billing is already finished.
steps.insight: Offline catch-up requires suitable durability or retained history; ephemeral broadcast is insufficient.

steps.title: Resume the slow subscriber
steps.caption: Shipping returns and receives its retained event.
steps.insight: One slow independent consumer need not block unrelated completed billing work.

steps.title: Record the second reaction
steps.caption: Shipping records its effect and acknowledges its own delivery.
steps.insight: Two expected business reactions are not duplicate handling of one queue job.

steps.title: Inspect the complete path
steps.caption: Both subscriptions completed independently with explicit recovery behavior.
steps.insight: Measure subscriber lag and failures separately rather than reporting one generic event-success count.

title: CDC: capture commits, update views, and replay safely
objective: Keep a search view updated without independently double-writing every application request.
scenario: A price commit reaches search after lag, then appears again during connector recovery.
tradeoff: CDC reduces repeated scans but adds lag, schema coupling, log retention, and replay responsibilities.

steps.title: Change the source
steps.caption: The writer updates product 42; the transaction has not yet been acknowledged.
steps.insight: The source database, not search, decides whether the original write commits.

steps.title: Commit durably
steps.caption: The transaction log records the commit before successful acknowledgement.
steps.insight: A source commit does not imply immediate downstream visibility.

steps.title: Read the committed change
steps.caption: The connector reads position 100 after its checkpoint.
steps.insight: A restart position is part of the data pipelineâ€™s correctness, not just performance.

steps.title: Publish downstream
steps.caption: E10 reaches the change stream while search still has version nine.
steps.insight: Each stage can introduce lag even while all processes are healthy.

steps.title: A consumer stalls
steps.caption: The consumer pauses; source writes continue but search freshness degrades.
steps.insight: Watch retained-log growth as well as destination lag.

steps.title: Apply and checkpoint
steps.caption: The consumer updates product 42 and records recoverable progress.
steps.insight: Coordinate the index effect and replay behavior; do not assume transport delivery is exactly once.

steps.title: Return the updated view
steps.caption: A search reader now sees price 550.
steps.insight: Measure commit-to-visible delay, not just connector request latency.
detail: Source and view have different roles

steps.title: Restart from an older point
steps.caption: Recovery resumes before E10 and emits it again.
steps.insight: Replaying a durable log is expected recovery behavior.
detail: A lost log segment needs a plan

steps.title: Keep the result correct
steps.caption: The version rule makes repeated E10 harmless; search remains at 550.
steps.insight: Batching can reduce overhead, but its waiting time still counts toward freshness.

title: Event sourcing: history is authoritative, views are rebuildable
objective: Preserve business history and reconstruct state without repeating external side effects.
scenario: An account deposits 100, withdraws 30, then rebuilds a lost balance view.
tradeoff: History enables audit and replay, but schemas, concurrency, snapshots, and side effects need deliberate handling.

steps.title: Validate the command
steps.caption: The handler checks the deposit and its expected account history version.
steps.insight: Business decisions belong before the durable event append.

steps.title: Append the first fact
steps.caption: Deposited(100) is durably appended as event one.
steps.insight: Concurrent appends need a version or serialization rule, not blind competing histories.
detail: A notification alone is not sourcing

steps.title: Build the current view
steps.caption: The projector applies event one; the derived balance becomes 100.
steps.insight: The balance view is a useful copy, not the only business history.

steps.title: Send a live receipt
steps.caption: An independent sender handles the live event once under its deduplication policy.
steps.insight: External actions must not be blindly repeated by a view rebuild.

steps.title: Append the withdrawal
steps.caption: A valid withdrawal appends event two after version one.
steps.insight: Check invariants against authoritative history or serialized aggregate state.

steps.title: Derive the new balance
steps.caption: Applying both events gives the current balance of 70.
steps.insight: Stored facts and calculated state are different representations.

steps.title: Lose only the view
steps.caption: The balance view is lost, but the durable event history survives.
steps.insight: A rebuildable projection reduces data-loss risk only when the history itself is protected.

steps.title: Replay without side effects
steps.caption: The projector replays deposit and withdrawal; receipts are not replayed with it.
steps.insight: Rebuilds derive state; live side effects require their own explicit processing rules.

steps.title: Serve the rebuilt result
steps.caption: The client reads 70 again from the restored view.
steps.insight: Event sourcing is useful when historical facts justify its extra evolution and recovery work.

title: CQRS: separate writes from query-shaped read views
objective: Optimize read and write responsibilities separately while making projection lag visible.
scenario: Order 42 commits before its asynchronously updated order-list view includes it.
tradeoff: Separate models can simplify access patterns but add synchronization, lag, and rebuild work.

nodes.label: Transactional outbox
nodes.role: Event in the same DB commit

steps.title: Use the write path
steps.caption: The customer submits a create command with required validation.
steps.insight: CQRS separates responsibilities; it does not require event sourcing.

steps.title: Commit order and handoff
steps.caption: Order 42 and its outbox record commit together.
steps.insight: The outbox closes one crash gap between a database write and publishing its update.

steps.title: Return the committed ID
steps.caption: The command returns order 42 before the projection finishes.
steps.insight: Truthful acknowledgement can identify a committed order without claiming every view is current.
detail: UI can show a pending view

steps.title: Read the old projection
steps.caption: An immediate list query reads the still-old order-list view.
steps.insight: Read-model lag is not proof that the original command failed.
detail: Do not create another order blindly
A read view is a separate model

steps.title: Deliver the update
steps.caption: The outbox publisher supplies committed E42 to the projector.
steps.insight: Projection delivery can repeat; define recoverable progress.

steps.title: Build a query-shaped row
steps.caption: The projector updates the customer-specific listing.
steps.insight: Optimize this view for real queries instead of forcing each screen through write-model joins.

steps.title: Serve the updated list
steps.caption: The next query returns order 42 from the read model.
steps.insight: A useful read model can be rebuilt; it is not necessarily the primary source of truth.

steps.title: Replay safely after recovery
steps.caption: A repeated E42 leaves the same listing rather than creating another order row.
steps.insight: Separate models create extra operational work; simple CRUD may not need this split.
detail: Define how to rebuild the view

title: Circuit breaker: stop cascading calls, then test recovery
objective: Limit repeated calls to a failing dependency while preserving truthful business outcomes.
scenario: A checkout calls a payment service that begins timing out.
tradeoff: Fail-fast behavior preserves resources but rejects or delays useful work until the dependency recovers.

steps.title: Closed permits calls
steps.caption: Checkout reaches payment through a closed breaker with a bounded deadline.
steps.insight: A breaker observes a failure pattern; a timeout bounds an individual call.

steps.title: Timeout creates uncertainty
steps.caption: A payment call times out; its business result may still be unknown.
steps.insight: A timeout is not proof that the payment never happened.
detail: Do not invent a successful charge

steps.title: Open after the policy
steps.caption: Repeated failures meet the configured opening rule.
steps.insight: Opening is based on an explicit policy, not one universal failure count.

steps.title: Fail fast on the next call
steps.caption: The open breaker refuses another call before it reaches payment.
steps.insight: Stopping repeated calls can prevent cascading resource exhaustion.

steps.title: Preserve business truth
steps.caption: Checkout records pending or unavailable and returns a clear response.
steps.insight: The fallback must preserve business correctness, not merely return HTTP success.

steps.title: Permit limited probes
steps.caption: After cooldown, half-open allows only controlled recovery probes.
steps.insight: Unbounded probes could immediately recreate the original overload.

steps.title: Close after recovery
steps.caption: A successful probe satisfies the selected recovery policy.
steps.insight: A failed probe would reopen the breaker under its policy.

steps.title: Resolve earlier unknown work
steps.caption: Checkout queries the durable payment outcome before settling order 42.
steps.insight: Closing the breaker does not automatically resolve payments whose responses were lost.

title: Discovery: find instances, detect suspicion, and route safely
objective: Find changing service instances without assuming that discovered health remains current.
scenario: A caller discovers orders A and B; A fails before the next request.
tradeoff: Cached discovery reduces lookups but delays changes; fast failure detection increases false-suspicion risk.

steps.title: Publish available instances
steps.caption: A and B register addresses and report health information.
steps.insight: A heartbeat proves recent reachability, not every business dependencyâ€™s health.

steps.title: Discover candidates
steps.caption: The resolver returns its candidate endpoint set to the caller.
steps.insight: Discovery finds destinations; load-balancing policy chooses among them.

steps.title: Call a selected instance
steps.caption: The caller reads order 42 from A successfully.
steps.insight: A successful past request cannot guarantee the next request will succeed.

steps.title: An endpoint becomes stale
steps.caption: A fails after discovery, but the caller still has its old address.
steps.insight: A registry response is a point-in-time observation.

steps.title: Bound the failed call
steps.caption: The next call to A times out rather than waiting forever.
steps.insight: A timeout can indicate failure or delay; it is not infallible proof of a crash.
detail: A write may have an unknown outcome

steps.title: Mark A suspect
steps.caption: Health policy times out A and stops advertising it as eligible.
steps.insight: Detection thresholds trade response speed against false alarms.

steps.title: Refresh the candidate set
steps.caption: A bounded refresh replaces the callerâ€™s stale candidates with B.
steps.insight: A long-lived client must have a way to learn membership changes.

steps.title: Use a safe retry
steps.caption: The caller sends the safe order read to B and receives a result.
steps.insight: A payment write needs an idempotency or reconciliation policy before retrying another instance.
detail: Routing does not prove business safety

title: Disaster recovery: recover data and restore useful service
objective: Choose and test separate targets for recoverable data loss and service restoration time.
scenario: A regional outage follows a 10:00 backup and logs recoverable through 10:15.
tradeoff: More recoverable logs reduce potential data loss; faster tested restoration reduces outage time, usually at extra cost.

steps.title: Define targets first
steps.caption: This example targets at most 15 minutes lost data and 30 minutes outage.
steps.insight: RPO and RTO are requirements, not automatically guaranteed backup properties.

steps.title: Capture recoverable state
steps.caption: A snapshot reaches the vault; later logs are archived through 10:15.
steps.insight: Recoverability requires usable copies that survive the same disaster.

steps.title: The region fails at 10:20
steps.caption: Customers lose primary service; newer data lacks a recoverable log copy.
steps.insight: The outage clock begins at loss of useful service.

steps.title: Backup alone misses target
steps.caption: Restoring only the 10:00 snapshot risks twenty minutes of lost changes.
steps.insight: The snapshot-only recovery point misses this exampleâ€™s fifteen-minute loss target.

steps.title: Replay available logs
steps.caption: Logs advance restored state to 10:15, leaving five minutes potentially lost.
steps.insight: The achieved recovery point meets the chosen RPO here; it is not the targetâ€™s definition.

steps.title: Restore the whole service
steps.caption: Application configuration and database restoration finish at 10:50.
steps.insight: Files restored does not necessarily mean users can complete checkout.

steps.title: Validate before routing
steps.caption: Recovery checks test useful requests and data invariants.
steps.insight: Exercise real business behavior rather than relying only on a process-is-running signal.
detail: Do not route to an unready restore

steps.title: Switch traffic at 11:00
steps.caption: Customers regain service forty minutes after the outage began.
steps.insight: The observed forty-minute recovery misses this exampleâ€™s thirty-minute RTO.

steps.title: Improve the right mechanism
steps.caption: More recoverable capture affects loss; faster rehearsed recovery affects downtime.
steps.insight: Choose improvements by the missed business target, not the number of backup files.

title: OAuth and OIDC: delegated access without sharing passwords
objective: Delegate API permissions and establish login identity without confusing token purposes or audiences.
scenario: A photo-printing client signs a user in and requests permitted photos.
tradeoff: Delegation avoids sharing a password but requires redirect, token, lifetime, scope, and ownership validation.

steps.title: Request limited access
steps.caption: The client redirects with the selected scopes and flow protections.
steps.insight: Permission requests should name needed access rather than ask for unlimited data.

steps.title: Sign in at the provider
steps.caption: The user authenticates at the provider, not by giving the client a password.
steps.insight: OAuth authorization and user authentication are related but different jobs.

steps.title: Return a short-lived code
steps.caption: The browser returns an authorization code to the registered client callback.
steps.insight: A callback code is not the access token to present to the photo API.
detail: Do not redeem an unrelated code

steps.title: Exchange the code
steps.caption: The client supplies the code and required verifier or client authentication.
steps.insight: Exact checks depend on the client type and selected standard flow.

steps.title: Validate the login identity
steps.caption: For OIDC, the client validates the ID token intended for that client.
steps.insight: An ID token conveys client login identity; it is not a generic API permission token.
detail: Check nonce and lifetime as required

steps.title: Request the permitted photo
steps.caption: The client sends the access token to its intended photo API.
steps.insight: API authorization includes both token permission and the requested objectâ€™s ownership.
detail: Do not substitute an ID token

steps.title: Return authorized data
steps.caption: The API returns the allowed photo through the client.
steps.insight: Sign-in and token receipt do not prove every object is accessible.

steps.title: Reject an unrelated photo
steps.caption: The same signed-in user asks for a photo owned by someone else.
steps.insight: A valid identity does not grant unlimited access.

steps.title: Respect token lifetime
steps.caption: Expired access requires an allowed renewal flow or a new authorization.
steps.insight: Renewal is a defined protocol behavior; refresh credentials are not universally issued.

title: SSO: reuse provider login, keep application sessions explicit
objective: Reuse one identity-provider login across applications without assuming one universal session or logout.
scenario: An employee opens payroll and email, then logs out of payroll.
tradeoff: Central sign-in improves reuse, but application permissions, session lifetimes, and global revocation still need coordination.

steps.title: Open the first application
steps.caption: Payroll redirects the browser to the trusted identity provider.
steps.insight: An application relies on an agreed identity protocol, not another appâ€™s password store.

steps.title: Authenticate once
steps.caption: The employee signs in at the provider and receives a provider session.
steps.insight: The provider session is separate from application sessions.

steps.title: Establish payroll access
steps.caption: Payroll validates the result and creates its own session.
steps.insight: Authenticated identity still needs payroll permission.

steps.title: Open another application
steps.caption: Email redirects through the same provider.
steps.insight: The provider can recognize its existing session instead of demanding a new password.

steps.title: Create a second app session
steps.caption: Email validates its result and establishes an independent session.
steps.insight: One sign-in can produce multiple independent application sessions.
detail: Each app controls its own session

steps.title: Log out of payroll only
steps.caption: Payroll invalidates its session after the employee selects logout.
steps.insight: Local logout is not universal logout unless that policy is implemented.

steps.title: Email still works
steps.caption: The browser accesses email using its still-valid email session.
steps.insight: This follows independent session boundaries, not a failure of SSO.
detail: Provider may still be signed in
Payroll may sign in again on reopening

steps.title: Design global revocation
steps.caption: Organization-wide sign-out needs explicit provider and application-session rules.
steps.insight: Disabling an account does not inherently end every already-established application session immediately.

title: TLS and mTLS: protect connections, then authorize the operation
objective: Protect data in transit and verify peers without confusing identity with record-level permission.
scenario: A browser requests an order through a gateway and an internal orders service.
tradeoff: Connection reuse can reduce handshake work, but verification and operation-level authorization must remain enforced.

steps.title: Identify the external server
steps.caption: The browser receives the gateway certificate during TLS setup.
steps.insight: HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS; a certificate helps authenticate the connection peer.

steps.title: Use local trust rules
steps.caption: The browser validates the certificate with its trust configuration.
steps.insight: This trust node is local configuration, not a required online CA call for every request.

steps.title: Carry the request securely
steps.caption: The protected browser connection carries the HTTP order request.
steps.insight: TLS protects this hop; terminating it does not automatically protect another internal hop.

steps.title: Authenticate internal peers
steps.caption: The gateway verifies the service; the service verifies the gateway certificate.
steps.insight: mTLS authenticates both connection peers under their certificate rules.

steps.title: Authorize the requested item
steps.caption: The service evaluates the userâ€™s permission to read order 42.
steps.insight: An authenticated gateway is not automatic permission for every end-user operation.

steps.title: Return the permitted result
steps.caption: The allowed order response travels over the protected hops.
steps.insight: Encryption and authorization solve different parts of the end-to-end problem.

steps.title: Deny another userâ€™s order
steps.caption: A valid connection requests an order outside the userâ€™s permissions.
steps.insight: Valid certificates do not grant unlimited access.

steps.title: Fail a bad certificate
steps.caption: A later invalid peer certificate prevents normal protected application traffic.
steps.insight: Faster handshakes must not come from disabling verification.

title: Nearby search: index candidates, then verify real proximity
objective: Find nearby eligible drivers without missing neighbors across a spatial cell boundary.
scenario: A rider in (2,1) needs a nearby driver across the boundary in (3,1).
tradeoff: Finer cells reduce candidates but increase lookups and update work; exact distance and freshness still need checks.

steps.title: Place the search correctly
steps.caption: The rider is near the right edge of cell (2,1).
steps.insight: A cell identifier is a candidate-search aid, not a physical distance measurement.

steps.title: Notice the adjacent driver
steps.caption: The closest driver lies just across the boundary in cell (3,1).
steps.insight: Nearby coordinates can have different cell labels.
detail: Different cell does not mean far
A quadtree has region boundaries too

steps.title: Try an incomplete query
steps.caption: Searching only the rider cell misses that driver.
steps.insight: The missing result comes from incomplete candidate coverage.
detail: Do not filter on prefix alone
A missed ID cannot pass later filtering

steps.title: Cover the search area
steps.caption: Query the relevant neighboring regions that intersect the search area.
steps.insight: Choose region coverage for the actual radius instead of one matching prefix.

steps.title: Load candidate positions
steps.caption: The index returns driver IDs; retrieve positions and timestamps.
steps.insight: Index membership alone does not prove distance or current availability.

steps.title: Check distance and policy
steps.caption: Calculate actual distances and remove stale, unavailable, or out-of-range drivers.
steps.insight: Use geometry and business eligibility after narrowing candidates.

steps.title: Return an eligible match
steps.caption: Ranked results include the close driver across the cell boundary.
steps.insight: The end-to-end result combines indexing, current records, and exact filtering.
detail: A candidate is not a reservation

steps.title: Tune the actual workload
steps.caption: Measure candidate counts and location-update costs before changing precision.
steps.insight: Geohash precision or quadtree splits trade query work against maintenance and neighboring-region work.

title: Raft: commit one replicated history despite a minority partition
objective: Agree on a committed operation order under stated crash-fault and communication assumptions.
scenario: Three voters replicate configuration changes; the old leader becomes isolated.
tradeoff: A communicating majority can progress; losing a majority sacrifices progress to protect committed-history safety.

steps.title: Propose through the leader
steps.caption: The client sends X: set limit to 20, to leader A in term one.
steps.insight: An appended entry is not yet a committed or applied decision.
detail: Leader also stores its own entry

steps.title: Replicate to a majority
steps.caption: B durably acknowledges X; A and B form two of three voters.
steps.insight: Raft commits current-term entries using its majority and log rules, not arbitrary voting on values.

steps.title: Apply, then confirm
steps.caption: A applies committed X and returns the committed result.
steps.insight: Committed history drives deterministic state-machine application.

steps.title: Isolate the old leader
steps.caption: A appends Y: set limit to 30, but cannot contact a majority.
steps.insight: A minority cannot safely commit new entries just because its process is still running.
detail: Old leader may not know immediately

steps.title: Elect with log rules
steps.caption: B gets its own vote and Câ€™s eligible vote in a newer term.
steps.insight: Election requires majority votes and an up-to-date-log check.

steps.title: Retry with the new leader
steps.caption: The client retries the idempotent set; B appends Y in term two.

updates.c: C catches up: X then Y

steps.insight: The new leader may need to repair follower log prefixes before replication succeeds.
detail: Old term1 Y was not committed

steps.title: Commit a current-term entry
steps.caption: C acknowledges; B and C form a majority for term-two Y.
steps.insight: Quorum contact alone is insufficient: Raftâ€™s term and log conditions still apply.
detail: Majority is two of three here

steps.title: Apply and return success
steps.caption: B applies Y and confirms the new limit of 30.
steps.insight: Safety preserves one committed order while the isolated minority cannot progress.

steps.title: Repair the returning voter
steps.caption: A learns the newer term and replaces its conflicting uncommitted suffix.
steps.insight: Raft can discard conflicting uncommitted entries; committed history must not be overwritten.
detail: A steps down on newer term

title: Fencing: make the protected resource reject stale owners
objective: Prevent an expired lease holder from corrupting data after a newer owner takes over.
scenario: Worker A pauses; B takes over; A later resumes with an older token.
tradeoff: Leases coordinate ownership, but fencing works only when the protected resource durably enforces monotonic tokens.

steps.title: Acquire an ownership lease
steps.caption: A receives token 10 from an authority that issues increasing tokens.
steps.insight: A lease is a time-bounded ownership promise, not a mechanism that kills paused processes.

steps.title: Write under the first token
steps.caption: The store accepts Aâ€™s token-ten write and records its fence.
steps.insight: The protected store participates in safety by validating tokens, not merely trusting a worker.

steps.title: Pause beyond the lease
steps.caption: A pauses long enough that its lease expires.
steps.insight: Expiry changes the authorityâ€™s ownership state; it does not stop Aâ€™s future instructions.
detail: A can resume with old state

steps.title: Let another worker take over
steps.caption: The coordinator retries the same logical job on B.
steps.insight: A newer lease carries a higher fencing token than the old ownerâ€™s token.
detail: Token issuance needs a safety contract

steps.title: Advance the enforced fence
steps.caption: B writes with token 11; the store durably advances its fence.
