steps.insight: After observing eleven, the resource must refuse writes carrying older ownership.

steps.title: The old worker resumes
steps.caption: A wakes and sends a stale write carrying token 10.
steps.insight: Both processes can be running even though only one holds the current lease.

steps.title: Reject the stale effect
steps.caption: The store rejects token 10 because it is older than its stored fence 11.
steps.insight: The protected data remains safe because the resource enforces the ordering.

steps.title: Keep recovery explicit
steps.caption: The workflow records the rejected stale attempt without overwriting Bâ€™s result.
steps.insight: Fencing protects this resource; external side effects need their own idempotency and authorization rules.
detail: Every protected write needs a check
No resource check means no fencing

title: Gossip: membership spreads without instant agreement
objective: Spread membership observations efficiently while tolerating temporarily different node views.
scenario: A storage node joins while one existing peer is temporarily unreachable.
tradeoff: More exchanges reduce convergence delay but consume bandwidth; spreading observations does not establish consensus.

steps.title: A local view is not global
steps.caption: The client asks B for destinations before B has heard about D.
steps.insight: A useful local answer can still be temporarily incomplete.
detail: Each node holds its own view.

steps.title: D reaches one peer
steps.caption: D announces itself to A, creating a newer membership observation.
steps.insight: One successful announcement does not instantly update every peer.
detail: Other peers still have old views.

steps.title: A tells B
steps.caption: A exchanges the newer observation with a selected peer, B.
steps.insight: Periodic peer exchanges distribute the work of spreading knowledge.

steps.title: B tells C
steps.caption: B later relays the update, allowing C to learn about D.
steps.insight: Information travels over multiple exchanges rather than one universal broadcast.
detail: C learns through B, not D.

steps.title: A partition delays E
steps.caption: C cannot deliver the observation to E while their connection is unavailable.
steps.insight: A delayed observation is not proof that the remote process has died.
detail: E can remain alive but isolated.

steps.title: Communication recovers
steps.caption: A later successful exchange supplies E with the newer member information.
steps.insight: Convergence requires communication and the protocol rules to permit state propagation.

steps.title: Peers resynchronize
steps.caption: E exchanges state with A, helping reconcile their known observations.
steps.insight: A reconnecting peer needs version-aware reconciliation, not blind last-arrival wins.
detail: Old messages may return after recovery.

steps.title: Read after propagation
steps.caption: The client asks B again and can now discover the new node.
steps.insight: Observe convergence time and message volume before increasing gossip frequency.
detail: It does not order committed writes.

title: Availability: replace, reroute, and inspect dependencies
objective: Keep a required operation reachable when individual components fail.
scenario: Checkout has two application instances but shares one database.
tradeoff: Redundancy needs spare capacity and working failover; shared dependencies can still stop both instances.

steps.title: Trace a working checkout
steps.caption: The customer reaches A, which commits the order in the shared database.
steps.insight: Measure the whole operation, not just whether an instance responds.
detail: A successful process ping is narrower.

steps.title: Instance A fails
steps.caption: A stops serving; the monitor observes failed readiness checks.
steps.insight: Having B does not help until callers stop routing new work to A.

steps.title: Remove A from routing
steps.caption: The router learns that B is the usable destination.
steps.insight: Readiness information must actually affect the traffic path.
detail: Retries must be safe for the write.

steps.title: The survivor needs room
steps.caption: B handles A's replacement load and still depends on database capacity.
steps.insight: Failover can overload a survivor that lacks spare capacity.
detail: Two instances do not double DB capacity.
Tail latency can rise under overload.

steps.title: The shared database fails
steps.caption: B loses the shared database; restoring A would not repair checkout.
steps.insight: Application redundancy does not remove a shared database failure point.
detail: A fast error is not checkout success.

steps.title: Degrade by operation
steps.caption: B can serve cached public products while checkout reports temporary failure.
steps.insight: State which product function still works instead of claiming universal availability.
detail: Do not invent a successful payment.

steps.title: Recover and verify
steps.caption: After database recovery, readiness and real checkout behavior are checked again.
steps.insight: Recovery is complete when the required operation works safely again.
detail: Avoid sending all traffic at once.

steps.title: Measure the promise
steps.caption: The customer receives a real checkout result through the healthy path.
steps.insight: Track successful operations and latency under failures, not server counts alone.

title: Indexes: narrow a query without forgetting write cost
objective: Reduce unnecessary record examination for a demonstrated access pattern.
scenario: A customer requests ten recent orders from a large order table.
tradeoff: Useful indexes can speed selected reads while consuming storage and adding maintenance work to writes.

steps.title: State the access pattern
steps.caption: The API asks for one customer's newest ten orders, not every order.
steps.insight: An index should serve an actual filter, ordering, and result size.
detail: A bounded page limits returned work.

steps.title: Measure the starting plan
steps.caption: Without a suitable access path, many unrelated records may be examined.
steps.insight: Separate rows examined from rows returned when locating expensive work.
detail: A small test table can hide the cost.

steps.title: Consider a matching index
steps.caption: An index beginning with customer and creation time offers a narrower path.
steps.insight: A matching index may avoid scanning unrelated customer records.
detail: Column order matters to this query.

steps.title: Locate the needed records
steps.caption: The selected range leads to the records needed for the page.
steps.insight: An index is an access structure, not a second independent source of truth.
detail: Some plans still fetch table rows.
Not every query uses this index.

steps.title: Return and compare
steps.caption: The API returns the page and compares query timing with the original workload.
steps.insight: Verify the actual plan and latency rather than assuming index presence means improvement.

steps.title: Writes maintain the index
steps.caption: A newly created order changes both stored records and the index structure.
steps.insight: Read acceleration creates extra write and storage work.

steps.title: Another query may scan
steps.caption: A broad filter may make scanning preferable to many individual lookups.
steps.insight: The planner can reasonably choose a different access path for a different query.
detail: Do not force one universal index.

steps.title: Keep evidence, not clutter
steps.caption: Compare read gain, write latency, storage, and the workloads each index supports.
steps.insight: Remove only genuinely unused indexes after checking all relevant query workloads.

title: CDN: origin content, nearby reuse, and freshness
objective: Serve safely reusable content near viewers while reducing origin transfers.
scenario: Two viewers request a popular image that a publisher later replaces.
tradeoff: Caching lowers repeated origin work but introduces freshness, access-control, and regional cold-miss decisions.

steps.title: Publish the original
steps.caption: The publisher stores logo v1 at the origin with a deliberate caching policy.
steps.insight: A CDN serves origin content under a cache and access policy, not arbitrary private data.

steps.title: The first viewer misses
steps.caption: A's nearby edge has no usable copy and asks the origin.
steps.insight: Cold requests still reach origin storage and may include long-distance transfer.
detail: A CDN does not erase the origin.

steps.title: Fill and respond
steps.caption: Origin bytes reach the edge, which stores an allowed copy and responds to A.
steps.insight: The edge can reuse only the responses its keys and policy permit.

steps.title: Reuse near the viewer
steps.caption: B asks for the same safe cache key and receives the edge copy.
steps.insight: A warm hit reduces origin traffic and repeated distance, not personalized query cost.

steps.title: The origin changes
steps.caption: The publisher replaces bytes under the old name while the edge still holds v1.
steps.insight: Updating origin bytes does not instantly replace existing cached copies.
detail: An old copy can outlive the update.

steps.title: Invalidate the old cache key
steps.caption: The publisher invalidates the old key; the next request fetches v2 from the origin.
steps.insight: Choose versioning, expiry, or invalidation for the product's freshness requirement.
detail: Versioned names change the cache key.

steps.title: Keep private data private
steps.caption: A private invoice must not reuse a public image-style cache key and policy.
steps.insight: Authentication and private variants must be designed before permitting shared reuse.
detail: A high hit rate cannot justify leakage.

steps.title: Verify the whole benefit
steps.caption: Compare viewer response time and origin traffic for warm and cold requests.
steps.insight: Test geography, updates, outages, and access behavior alongside cache hit rate.
detail: Cached public content may survive outage.
A slow database query needs other work.

title: P2P: exchange verified pieces and survive departures
objective: Distribute content-serving work while verifying pieces and tolerating peers leaving.
scenario: A new downloader exchanges file pieces with peers, then loses one source.
tradeoff: Peer upload capacity reduces origin load but introduces discovery, integrity, reachability, and scarce-piece challenges.

steps.title: Find potential sources
steps.caption: C obtains candidate peers instead of asking the origin for every byte.
steps.insight: Discovery helps locate peers but does not prove they are reachable or trustworthy.

steps.title: Know what to verify
steps.caption: C retrieves trusted metadata identifying the expected file pieces.
steps.insight: A matching untrusted file and untrusted checksum do not establish authenticity.

steps.title: Receive useful pieces
steps.caption: A sends pieces 1 and 2, which C verifies before keeping.
steps.insight: A peer can serve data it already has without holding the entire file.
detail: Transfers can be resumed by piece.

steps.title: Obtain another piece
steps.caption: B provides piece 3 while C still lacks piece 4.
steps.insight: Different peers contribute different parts of the same logical content.
detail: Track which pieces are still missing.

steps.title: Become a source too
steps.caption: C uploads verified piece 3 to A rather than only consuming bandwidth.
steps.insight: Participants can provide as well as consume, spreading origin-serving work.
detail: Sharing does not imply no servers.

steps.title: A source disappears
steps.caption: B leaves before C receives its remaining piece.
steps.insight: Churn and scarce pieces can delay completion even after most bytes arrive.
detail: More peers need not hold every piece.

steps.title: Recover missing content
steps.caption: C finds piece 4 at the origin and verifies the fallback transfer.
steps.insight: Alternative sources and resumable progress keep one departure from discarding all work.
detail: Trust checks apply to every source.

steps.title: Measure the real exchange
steps.caption: C assembles the file while the system measures origin traffic and completion time.
steps.insight: Optimize useful pieces, reachability, and upload cost rather than counting peers alone.

title: URL shortener: create, resolve, cache, and disable
objective: Create unique aliases and serve redirect-heavy traffic with explicit freshness and abuse rules.
scenario: A campaign link becomes viral, then its owner disables it.
tradeoff: Caches reduce database reads but complicate editing, disabling, miss bursts, and client-side freshness.

steps.title: Define the write first
steps.caption: The owner submits a destination to the creation API for validation.
steps.insight: A short-link system needs a write contract, not only a fast redirect path.
detail: A short code is not authorization.

steps.title: Propose and reserve a code
steps.caption: The API gets a candidate and attempts a unique database insertion.
steps.insight: The authoritative store must prevent two links from sharing one code.
detail: Do not overwrite an existing mapping.

steps.title: Recover a collision
steps.caption: A collision causes a new candidate attempt rather than corruption.
steps.insight: Collision handling belongs on the creation path before a link is published.

steps.title: Publish the saved alias
steps.caption: The successful database write lets the API return the alias to its owner.
steps.insight: Return creation success only after the required persistence guarantee is satisfied.

steps.title: First redirect misses
steps.caption: A visitor reaches the redirect service; the cache miss triggers a database lookup.
steps.insight: A cache miss still consumes origin capacity and adds read latency.
detail: Read mapping status, not URL alone.
Unknown codes need a defined response.

steps.title: Respond without analytics
steps.caption: The mapping is cached, the visitor is redirected, and analytics work is queued.
steps.insight: Delayed analytics can stay off the redirect critical path when the product permits it.

steps.title: Viral traffic reuses data
steps.caption: Repeated visitors use the cached mapping instead of repeating every database read.
steps.insight: At 20k requests/s and 95% hits, simplified database read load is 1k/s.
detail: A hot key can overload a cache node.

steps.title: Disable and invalidate
steps.caption: The owner disables the link and the API invalidates the known cache entry.
steps.insight: Server and browser caches need a deliberate policy for disablement freshness.
detail: An origin change is not instant purge.

steps.title: Resolve against current state
steps.caption: The next miss reads disabled state and returns an unavailable result.
steps.insight: Optimize reload bursts without losing the mapping's correctness and abuse rules.
detail: Test updates and cache outage behavior.

title: Messaging: durable acceptance, routing, and reconnect
objective: Deliver durable messages across intermittent connections with explicit retry and acknowledgement meanings.
scenario: A recipient reconnects after receiving a message but losing its acknowledgement.
tradeoff: Durability, per-conversation order, fanout cost, and fast delivery require different coordination and scaling choices.

steps.title: Keep media off chat work
steps.caption: The sender stores an attachment once and obtains its authorized reference.
steps.insight: Repeated message delivery should not require copying the attachment through every worker.
detail: Media has its own access policy.

steps.title: Persist a stable message ID
steps.caption: The gateway records m41 and coordinates its pending delivery event.
steps.insight: A lost response must not turn a sender retry into another logical message.

steps.title: Accepted is not delivered
steps.caption: The store confirms acceptance and the sender receives that precise status.
steps.insight: A server acceptance guarantee is different from recipient receipt or read status.

steps.title: Queue and locate delivery
steps.caption: A worker receives pending work and checks the connection directory.
steps.insight: Offline handling requires durable retrieval or retry, not a permanently open socket.
detail: A queue does not add infinite capacity.

steps.title: Reconnect elsewhere
steps.caption: The recipient establishes a new session, which becomes discoverable for delivery.
steps.insight: Connection location and message history have different responsibilities.
detail: Do not query every connection server.

steps.title: Deliver with a lost receipt
steps.caption: m41 reaches the phone, but its acknowledgement is lost.
steps.insight: Delivery attempts can repeat even when the first attempt reached the user.
detail: The network can lose the response.

steps.title: Retry without another bubble
steps.caption: The worker sends m41 again and the recipient recognizes its existing identifier.
steps.insight: Stable identifiers and durable rules prevent retries from becoming duplicate visible messages.
detail: Do not infer global chat ordering.

steps.title: Record the delivery meaning
steps.caption: A receipt updates status and informs the sender that the recipient received m41.
steps.insight: Each displayed receipt should correspond to an explicitly defined event.

steps.title: Plan group fanout capacity
steps.caption: A large group multiplies delivery attempts and can grow queue age.
steps.insight: 100 messages/s to 2,000 recipients imply roughly 200k delivery attempts/s before retries.

title: Feeds: publish, fan out, read, and enforce visibility
objective: Serve follower feeds while balancing publication fanout, reading work, freshness, and visibility.
scenario: Ordinary posts and a celebrity post compete with delayed timeline workers.
tradeoff: Precomputing feeds reduces read work but amplifies writes; merging large authors at read time shifts cost back to reads.

steps.title: Store the original post
steps.caption: The post API records authoritative content, access rules, and recoverable fanout intent.
steps.insight: Publication acceptance does not prove every follower timeline is updated.
detail: Keep a durable source of content.
Persist intent with the post commit.

steps.title: Distribute references later
steps.caption: A queue decouples publication from follower timeline work.
steps.insight: Asynchronous precomputation adds a measurable post-to-feed delay.

steps.title: Precompute ordinary feeds
steps.caption: The worker adds P references to the followers' timelines.
steps.insight: References avoid copying full post content into every timeline.

steps.title: Read a bounded page
steps.caption: A follower asks the feed API for a page of timeline references.
steps.insight: Pagination bounds work instead of fetching an entire lifetime feed.
detail: A reference is not the content.
Feed ordering is an explicit choice.

steps.title: Fetch currently allowed posts
steps.caption: The API resolves content and current access before returning the page.
steps.insight: An old timeline reference must not bypass current deletion or privacy rules.
detail: Cache with the right user context.
Check access at the content boundary.

steps.title: A celebrity changes the cost
steps.caption: A huge follower count turns one publication into a large distribution burst.
steps.insight: Average followers per post can hide the worst write bursts.

steps.title: Choose a mixed strategy
steps.caption: Ordinary authors remain precomputed; large-author content is merged during reads.
steps.insight: A mixed design reduces massive write bursts while increasing read-path work.
detail: Use measured fanout and read frequency.
Do not copy an arbitrary threshold.

steps.title: A deleted post lingers
steps.caption: The author disables P while a timeline reference still exists.
steps.insight: Reference cleanup and access enforcement are different tasks.
detail: Never expose a forbidden cached copy.

steps.title: Return and measure the choice
steps.caption: The feed excludes forbidden content and measures read latency and publication lag.
steps.insight: Assess feed-read latency, timeline writes, and post-to-feed delay together.
detail: Cheaper reads can mean more writes.
Fresher feeds may need extra work.

title: Video: prepare renditions, then serve media nearby
objective: Prepare video safely and serve repeated media segments without making playback wait for encoding.
scenario: A new title launches while regional CDN caches are still cold.
tradeoff: More renditions improve adaptation but increase encoding and storage; regional caching introduces cold-miss and access-policy costs.

steps.title: Persist before preparation
steps.caption: The upload API stores the original before starting background preparation.
steps.insight: Upload and playback are different workloads with different readiness guarantees.
detail: Do not encode on the playback request.

steps.title: Create separate renditions
steps.caption: Workers read the source and build versions for different device/network needs.
steps.insight: A rendition is one resolution and bitrate choice, not an extra user request.

steps.title: A worker stops midway
steps.caption: Partial output must not be advertised as playable content.
steps.insight: A successful file write alone does not prove a complete rendition is usable.
detail: Resume or retry with safe output keys.

steps.title: Retry and publish readiness
steps.caption: A successful retry finishes the required outputs and verifies readiness.
steps.insight: Expose a manifest only when its required media outputs can be served.
detail: Duplicate jobs must not corrupt media.

steps.title: Fetch the playback plan
steps.caption: The player obtains the manifest and available rendition choices.
steps.insight: The application describes playback; media bytes use the delivery path.
detail: Login API capacity is not media capacity.

steps.title: Cold edge reaches origin
steps.caption: The first regional request fetches a segment from media origin.
steps.insight: A cold CDN request still consumes origin capacity and network distance.

steps.title: Warm viewers reuse bytes
steps.caption: Later requests for reusable segments are served near viewers.
steps.insight: 2,000 viewers at 4 Mb/s imply roughly 8 Gb/s before overhead.
detail: Media bandwidth is a major constraint.
Do not count only application requests.

steps.title: Adapt to the connection
steps.caption: The player chooses an available lower bitrate when needed to reduce buffering.
steps.insight: Lower transfer demand can improve continuity at the cost of visual quality.

steps.title: Test a regional launch
steps.caption: Cold-miss bursts and origin pressure need bounds, not assumptions of a warm cache.
steps.insight: Measure quality, buffering, origin load, and cache geography together.
detail: Higher hit ratio alone is not success.

title: Ride matching: fresh candidates are not reservations
objective: Find nearby candidates and assign limited drivers without conflicting simultaneous reservations.
scenario: Two riders select one nearby driver while some location updates are delayed.
tradeoff: Fresher locations increase update load; spatial precision adds lookup cost, and assignment still requires authoritative coordination.

steps.title: Ingest changing locations
steps.caption: Drivers report observed positions through a location ingestion path.
steps.insight: Record observation age; receiving an old report now does not make its position fresh.

steps.title: Accept the ride requests
steps.caption: Two riders request matches through the ride API.
steps.insight: A matching result requires more than a nearby-driver lookup.

steps.title: Search beyond one cell
steps.caption: The matcher considers neighboring spatial regions and filters stale candidates.
steps.insight: A closer driver can lie across a cell boundary rather than inside the rider's cell.
detail: A fast stale answer can be wrong.

steps.title: Race one available driver
steps.caption: A and B both propose D1, but only one conditional claim can win.
steps.insight: The authoritative state transition prevents a shared candidate from becoming two assignments.
detail: Failed claims must be retried safely.

steps.title: Deliver an identified offer
steps.caption: The winning assignment creates an offer addressed to the driver.
steps.insight: Offer delivery and reservation state need explicit identifiers and timeout behavior.
detail: A reserved driver is not yet accepted.

steps.title: Handle a missing response
steps.caption: D1 becomes unreachable and the offer reaches its timeout policy.
steps.insight: Do not release or reuse state blindly if an acceptance can race the timeout.

steps.title: Try another eligible driver
steps.caption: After the allowed transition, the matcher conditionally claims D2 and sends a new offer.
steps.insight: A fallback candidate still needs a new authoritative claim.
detail: Do not reuse expired ownership blindly.

steps.title: Accept and confirm the trip
steps.caption: D2 accepts and the assignment store records the valid transition.

updates.riders: A has D2; B has own state

steps.insight: Only the current accepted assignment should produce a confirmed rider result.
detail: Old offer replies must be rejected.
Receipt and state change can race.

steps.title: Tune the busy city
steps.caption: Measure matching latency, location age, and hot-region load together.
steps.insight: Adaptive updates and partitions trade freshness, maintenance work, and boundary coordination.
detail: Equal areas can have unequal traffic.
More partitions are not a universal fix.

title: Concurrency: overlap work; parallelism: execute together
objective: Distinguish managing overlapping tasks from executing independent work simultaneously.
scenario: Two independent CPU tasks each require two equal work slots.
tradeoff: Concurrency can overlap waiting without extra cores; parallel speedup requires independent work and available execution resources.

steps.title: Use the same task workload
steps.caption: A and B each need two equal CPU work slots in this illustration.
steps.insight: Keep the workload fixed before comparing execution strategies.
detail: These slots are not a benchmark.

steps.title: Single core starts A
steps.caption: One core executes A's first slot while B remains pending.
steps.insight: Both tasks can be in progress over time without running simultaneously.
detail: One core executes one CPU slot here.

steps.title: Switch to B
steps.caption: The next single-core slot serves B instead of finishing all of A first.
steps.insight: Interleaving is concurrency, not evidence of simultaneous execution.
detail: B now also has unfinished work.

steps.title: Return to A
steps.caption: A receives its second slot and can complete.
steps.insight: Concurrency describes overlap in task lifetimes, including switching and waiting.
detail: Task A has used two slots.
B still needs its second slot.

steps.title: Single-core trial finishes
steps.caption: B completes in slot four; the collector returns both results.
steps.insight: Finishing more tasks does not imply each task had shorter latency.
detail: Total CPU work remains four slots.

steps.title: Repeat on two cores
steps.caption: The same independent tasks are assigned to separate available cores.
steps.insight: Parallelism needs actual simultaneous execution capacity, not merely more queued tasks.
detail: Reset the trial, not the workload.
Do not assume every task is independent.

steps.title: Work at the same time
steps.caption: Core 1 serves A while core 2 serves B in the first parallel slot.
steps.insight: This simultaneous execution is parallelism.
detail: Two CPU slots happen at once.

steps.title: Compare completion and limits
steps.caption: Both tasks finish after two parallel slots under these simplified assumptions.
steps.insight: I/O waits can overlap with concurrency; CPU parallelism depends on resources and independent work.
detail: Same total work, different elapsed time.

title: Batch and stream: choose freshness and recovery rules
objective: Process event arrivals with the latency, cost, and recovery behavior the product actually needs.
scenario: Payments feed a periodic sales report and a live threshold alert.
tradeoff: Frequent streaming results reduce delay; batching amortizes work but waits, and both need safe recovery and late-data rules.

steps.title: Preserve the incoming events
steps.caption: Events are retained so consumers can process and recover from the same input.
steps.insight: Batch and stream describe processing choices, not whether input data must be durable.

steps.title: Process an early arrival
steps.caption: The stream path processes event 1 without waiting for the full report window.
steps.insight: Streaming can produce useful results while later events are still arriving.
detail: Output delay depends on actual work.

steps.title: Continue with the next input
steps.caption: Event 2 updates the live result while the batch job still waits.
steps.insight: Timely decisions and periodic reports can legitimately observe different processing progress.

steps.title: A live threshold is reached
steps.caption: Event 3 makes the running amount 60 and can trigger a configured live decision.
steps.insight: A live threshold use case values response time differently from a nightly report.
detail: Do not equate arrival with event time.

steps.title: Close a bounded batch
steps.caption: The batch job reads the three retained events for its selected report interval.
steps.insight: Batching waits so it can amortize work across a bounded collection.

steps.title: Publish the report
steps.caption: The batch publishes total 60 and records its own successful progress.
steps.insight: A report result is a product contract, not proof that the stream path used identical timing.
detail: A checkpoint is not the output itself.

steps.title: Recover after a crash
steps.caption: The stream resumes from a checkpoint that can cause event 3 to be seen again.
steps.insight: Output-before-checkpoint failures can repeat processing after recovery.
detail: A naive increment would double count.

steps.title: Protect repeated processing
steps.caption: The consumer recognizes an already applied event or uses an appropriate coordinated output rule.
steps.insight: Deduplication or transactional coordination must protect the actual output effect.
detail: Do not promise exactly-once by label.

steps.title: Choose the right path
steps.caption: Compare result delay, batch efficiency, recovery, and late-arriving event behavior.
steps.insight: The same system may use both paths for different requirements.
detail: Late events need an explicit policy.

title: Cache-through policies: load reads and persist writes
objective: Assign cache-loading and write-persistence responsibilities without assuming automatic freshness or atomicity.
scenario: A product price is read, updated, then read after a partial cache failure.
tradeoff: Read-through and write-through can coexist; synchronous persistence adds write latency and still needs partial-failure rules.

steps.title: Request data through a layer
steps.caption: The API asks the cache layer for a product instead of loading misses itself.
steps.insight: Read-through assigns missing-value loading to the cache layer.
detail: A cache layer has an explicit contract.

steps.title: The layer loads the miss
steps.caption: The cache layer fetches version 1 from the database.
steps.insight: A missing cached value still requires backing-store work.
detail: Preserve the right cache key inputs.
Loading can fail or be concurrent.

steps.title: Serve a reusable read
steps.caption: The cache returns the value and the API responds to the reader.
steps.insight: Read-through changes responsibility for loading, not the operation's freshness guarantee by itself.

steps.title: Submit a write-through edit
steps.caption: The authorized editor sends 550 through the same cache layer.
steps.insight: Write-through puts backing persistence on the synchronous write path.
detail: A pending write is not a success.
The layer must handle partial failure.

steps.title: Persist before success
steps.caption: After persistence succeeds, the layer can publish its new cached value under its policy.
steps.insight: Define what successful acknowledgement means across the layer and backing store.
detail: Read and write policies can combine.

steps.title: Handle a partial failure
steps.caption: A later backing write can commit even if the cache update or its response fails.
steps.insight: Synchronous calls do not magically create a transaction across every component.
detail: A timeout can hide a committed write.
Do not return an invented result.

steps.title: Recover under a clear rule
steps.caption: The API may use an authorized backing read when the layer's fallback policy permits it.
steps.insight: Fallback must preserve access and freshness requirements while respecting database capacity.

steps.title: Verify both operations
steps.caption: Reload a missing value and measure writes, stale reads, and outage behavior together.
steps.insight: Choose the policy from reuse, durability, and consistency needs rather than treating names as opposites.

title: Push and pull: who initiates learning about a change?
objective: Deliver state changes with an explicit initiator, retry contract, and acceptable detection delay.
scenario: A shop learns whether a payment finished using polling or a webhook.
tradeoff: Push can reduce unnecessary polls but needs trustworthy delivery and retries; pull trades polling load for detection delay.

steps.title: Pull asks before change
steps.caption: The shop polls the provider and receives pending status.
steps.insight: Pull means the receiver initiates a request for an update.
detail: A poll can return unchanged state.

steps.title: Authoritative state changes
steps.caption: The provider completes the payment before the shop necessarily learns about it.
steps.insight: A change happening and a consumer detecting it are separate events.
detail: Polling delay depends on its schedule.

steps.title: Push initiates a delivery
steps.caption: The provider sends a webhook event to the shop's registered endpoint.
steps.insight: Push means the sender initiates this notification, not that a permanent connection is required.

steps.title: Accept before acknowledging
steps.caption: The endpoint safely accepts processing work before returning its chosen acknowledgement.
steps.insight: Acknowledging too early can lose work if the receiver then crashes.
detail: The handler need not finish all work.
Durable acceptance has a defined point.

steps.title: Apply the business effect
steps.caption: A worker updates the order view using duplicate-safe event handling.
steps.insight: Webhook delivery does not replace authorization or business-state checks.
detail: Events can be delayed or reordered.

steps.title: A receipt can be lost
steps.caption: The provider may resend the same event if acknowledgement was not observed.
steps.insight: Retrying delivery must not repeat the logical payment effect.
detail: A successful first attempt can repeat.
Checking only in memory is fragile.

steps.title: Read what the shop knows
steps.caption: The application reads its local status, which may lag the provider.
steps.insight: A pushed event can still wait in a queue before becoming a readable local result.

steps.title: Compare with another poll
steps.caption: Polling remains a possible alternative or recovery check under the provider contract.
steps.insight: Choose detection delay, rate limits, delivery reliability, and operational complexity together.
detail: Pull controls when the receiver asks.

title: Sync and async: complete the order, then process email
objective: Separate the immediate operation guarantee from work allowed to complete later.
scenario: Checkout creates an order while its confirmation email may fail and retry.
tradeoff: Asynchronous work shortens required waiting but introduces delayed status, retries, and durable coordination responsibilities.

steps.title: Define checkout success
steps.caption: The client asks the API to create an order.
steps.insight: Decide whether success means durable order creation or also completed email delivery.
detail: A response must state its guarantee.
Not all follow-up work is essential.

steps.title: Coordinate order and event
steps.caption: The API records the order and a pending outbox event in one database transaction.
steps.insight: An outbox records the intent to publish alongside the business change.
detail: Avoid order saved but event lost.

steps.title: Return before email finishes
steps.caption: The API confirms the order while reporting email as pending.
steps.insight: Asynchronous completion does not mean pretending unfinished work already succeeded.
detail: The immediate order guarantee is met.
Email is a separate observable state.

steps.title: Relay committed work
steps.caption: A relay reads the committed outbox and submits an email event to the queue.
steps.insight: The relay decouples committed order state from queue availability.
detail: Retry the same logical event safely.

steps.title: Record publication progress
steps.caption: The relay records progress after the queue accepts the event.
steps.insight: A crash between publish and progress recording can produce duplicate delivery.
detail: The outbox does not erase retries.

steps.title: Email fails; order remains
steps.caption: The worker attempts the send, but the provider is unavailable.
steps.insight: A follow-up failure can leave the order valid while email is still pending.

steps.title: Retry the intended effect
steps.caption: The worker retries with a stable operation identity under the provider's contract.
steps.insight: External side effects need explicit duplicate and uncertain-response handling.
detail: A timeout may hide an accepted send.
Do not promise exactly-once by label.

steps.title: Expose later completion
steps.caption: Processing status is recorded so support or product views can explain the email outcome.
steps.insight: Useful asynchronous designs expose completion and failure rather than abandoning the job after acceptance.

steps.title: Contrast synchronous email
steps.caption: If the API sends email synchronously, the checkout response must wait for that result.
steps.insight: Synchronous versus asynchronous describes caller waiting, not whether the underlying work exists.
detail: A queue moves work; does not remove it.

title: API gateway: derive the boundary from the screen
objective: Choose where routing, shared request policies, and screen-specific composition belong.
scenario: Five services expose fifty APIs; this screen needs three results from different services.
tradeoff: An entry point simplifies client routing; optional aggregation adds coordination, latency, and a failure dependency.

steps.title: Start with three calls
steps.caption: The client calls only the three APIs this screen needs.
steps.insight: Fifty available APIs do not prove that a gateway is required.
detail: Two other services are not queried.

steps.title: Handle a slow response
steps.caption: Details and stock arrive, but reviews exceed the screen deadline.
steps.insight: Someone must own partial results even when the network calls are simple.

steps.title: Notice repeated work
steps.caption: Mobile and web clients both need routing, credentials, and failure policies.
steps.insight: Choose a boundary because a responsibility is repeated or fragile.
detail: Do not add components by API count.
A small client can keep direct calls.

steps.title: Introduce an entry point
steps.caption: A gateway routes a stable public request after shared policy checks.
steps.insight: Gateway routing and response composition are separate responsibilities.
detail: Routing alone does not merge results.

steps.title: Compose only if useful
steps.caption: A screen-specific aggregator requests the three independent results concurrently.
steps.insight: One client request can contain several downstream calls and their failure risks.

steps.title: Apply a response deadline
steps.caption: The aggregator receives required facts while reviews remain unavailable.
steps.insight: A partial-result policy makes the failure visible instead of inventing data.
detail: Reviews may be optional on this screen.

steps.title: Return an honest screen
steps.caption: The client receives details, stock, and an explicit unavailable-review status.
steps.insight: The screen contract determines whether partial success is useful.

steps.title: Account for the new risk
steps.caption: If the entry path fails, all requests using that path are affected.
steps.insight: Redundancy and recovery must match the dependency the design introduced.
detail: Use redundant entry points if required.

steps.title: Defend your choice
steps.caption: Keep the simplest arrangement that satisfies the actual screen and service requirements.
steps.insight: Revisit your first sketch: what became simpler, and what new failure did you accept?
detail: Gateway plus BFF is not mandatory.
